note: Lessons for the learning module. Synced into the database when the server starts (a lesson whose content changed gets version + 1). Exercise answers are compared after lower-casing and removing punctuation; an exercise with no accepted answers (or an answer that isn't one of them, for fill_blank and transform) is judged by the tutor.

lessons.title: Talking about yesterday
lessons.objective: Use the past simple of regular verbs (worked, played, called) to talk about yesterday.
lessons.summary: For finished actions in the past, add -ed to most verbs: work → worked, play → played, call → called.
lessons.explanation: When something happened and finished in the past — yesterday, last week, in 2020 — we use the past simple. For most verbs, just add -ed. If the verb ends in -e, add only -d (live → lived). The verb is the same for I, you, he, she, we and they.
examples: She called her mother last night.
We watched a film on Sunday.
They lived in Pune for two years.

exercises.prompt: Yesterday I ___ (walk) to the market.
Last Sunday we ___ (play) cricket.
Which sentence is correct?
exercises.explanation: Yesterday is finished, so we use the past simple: called.

exercises.prompt: Change to the past: "I clean my room."
Write one sentence about something you did yesterday, using a regular verb (like worked, cooked, watched).
exercises.explanation: Use a verb ending in -ed for a finished action.

lessons.title: Went, ate, saw: irregular past
lessons.objective: Use common irregular past forms (went, ate, saw, had, came, took, bought) correctly.
lessons.summary: Some common verbs don't take -ed in the past: go → went, eat → ate, see → saw, have → had, come → came, buy → bought.
lessons.explanation: Many everyday verbs have their own past form instead of -ed. We say "I went", not "I goed". These must be learnt one by one, but you already use the most common ones every day: went, ate, saw, had, came, took, bought, made, gave, got.
examples: I went to the office by bus.
He bought a new phone last month.

exercises.prompt: Last night we ___ (go) to a wedding.
I ___ (eat) idli this morning.
Which sentence is correct?
Change to the past: "She takes the train."
Write a sentence about your last holiday using went, saw or ate.

lessons.title: He works, she lives
lessons.objective: Add -s to the verb after he, she, it (and one person or thing) in the present simple.
lessons.summary: In the present simple, after he, she, it or one person, the verb takes -s: I work → he works.
lessons.explanation: For habits and facts we use the present simple. With I, you, we and they, the verb stays the same. With he, she, it — or one person like "my brother" — add -s (works, lives) or -es (watches, goes). have becomes has.
examples: My brother works in a bank.
He watches the news every night.

exercises.prompt: My sister ___ (work) in a hospital.
He ___ (go) to the gym every day.
Which sentence is correct?
Change "I drink tea" so it starts with "My father".
Write one sentence about what a family member does every day.
exercises.explanation: Remember the -s after he, she or one person.

lessons.title: A, an and the
lessons.objective: Choose a, an or the correctly in everyday sentences.
lessons.summary: a/an = one of many, first mention (a before consonant sounds, an before vowel sounds); the = a specific one we both know.
lessons.explanation: Use a or an when you talk about one thing for the first time, or any one of many: "I saw a dog." Use an before a vowel sound: an apple, an hour. Use the when it's clear which one: "The dog was big." or there is only one: the sun, the Prime Minister.
examples: She works in a school near my house.
The school has a big playground.

exercises.prompt: I ate ___ apple after lunch.
exercises.explanation: apple starts with a vowel sound → an.

exercises.prompt: My brother is ___ engineer.
exercises.explanation: engineer starts with a vowel sound → an.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct? "Can you switch off ___ fan, please?" (the fan in this room)
exercises.explanation: We both know which fan → the.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct? "I want to buy ___ new phone."
exercises.explanation: Any new phone, first mention → a.

exercises.prompt: Write two sentences about something you bought: first with a or an, then with the.
exercises.explanation: a/an the first time, the after that.

lessons.title: In, on, at for time
lessons.objective: Use at (times), on (days and dates) and in (months, years, parts of the day) correctly.
lessons.summary: at + a time (at 6 o'clock), on + a day or date (on Monday), in + a month, year or part of the day (in May, in the morning).
lessons.explanation: Think of it from small to big: at for an exact time (at 7:30, at night), on for a day or date (on Friday, on 15 August), in for longer periods (in June, in 2024, in the evening).
examples: We go to the village in May.

exercises.prompt: The train leaves ___ 5:45.
I have an interview ___ Monday.
Diwali is usually ___ October or November.
Which sentence is correct?
Write a sentence about your weekend plans using at, on or in.
exercises.explanation: at a time, on a day, in a month or part of the day.

lessons.title: Asking questions with do and does
lessons.objective: Make present-simple questions with do/does in the right word order.
lessons.summary: Question word + do/does + person + verb: Where do you live? What does she do?
lessons.explanation: In English questions, do or does comes before the person, and the main verb goes back to its basic form. Use does with he, she, it: "Where does he work?" (not "Where he works?"). For yes/no questions, start with do or does: "Do you like tea?"

exercises.prompt: Which question is correct?
___ your father work in Delhi?
Make a question: "She likes coffee." (start with Does)
Ask about the time the bank opens. Start with "What time".
accepted: What time does the bank open
exercises.explanation: What time + does + the bank + open.

exercises.prompt: Write two questions you could ask a new colleague.

lessons.title: Talking about your work
lessons.objective: Use common words and phrases to describe a job: work as, be in charge of, deal with, colleague, shift.
lessons.summary: I work as a… / I work in (a place) / I'm in charge of… / I deal with customers / I work the night shift.
lessons.explanation: Useful phrases: "I work as a nurse" (your job), "I work in a hospital" (the place), "I'm in charge of the accounts" (your responsibility), "I deal with customers" (handle), "my colleagues" (people you work with), "a shift" (fixed working hours).
examples: I work as a sales executive.
I work in a call centre in Gurugram.
I'm in charge of a team of five.

exercises.prompt: I work ___ a teacher.
Which word means the people you work with?
She is in ___ of the whole store.
Describe your job (or a job you want) in two sentences using at least one phrase from this lesson.
exercises.explanation: Try work as, work in, in charge of or deal with.

lessons.title: Have you ever…?
lessons.objective: Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) to talk about life experiences.
lessons.summary: have/has + past participle for experiences at any time in your life: I've been to Goa. Have you ever eaten sushi?
lessons.explanation: When the exact time doesn't matter — only that it happened in your life — use have or has with the past participle: been, seen, eaten, visited. With a finished time (yesterday, in 2019), use the past simple instead: "I went to Goa in 2019."
examples: She has never driven a car.

exercises.prompt: I have never ___ (see) the sea.
Which sentence is correct?
options: I have visited Mumbai last year.
I have visit Mumbai last year.
exercises.explanation: last year is a finished time → past simple.

exercises.prompt: Make a question with "ever": "You ate biryani in Hyderabad."
accepted: Have you ever eaten biryani in Hyderabad

exercises.prompt: Write one thing you have done and one thing you have never done.
